betterCitation: Heloise, The Letters of Abelard and Heloise, Letter 1, Heloise to Abelard (trans. Betty Radice, Penguin, 1974)
reason:
REFUTED ON THE LOCATOR. The wording is Radice's and I confirmed it. The letter number is wrong for the edition the source line names, and it is wrong in the worst way: in Betty Radice's Penguin of 1974, Letter 2 is a letter by Abelard, not by Heloise. A reader who follows this citation is sent to the wrong letter and the wrong author.

THE EVIDENCE. Internet Archive's catalogue record for the 1974 Penguin itself, item lettersofabelard00abel, Harmondsworth, Penguin, 1974, ISBN 0140442979, carries the MARC contents note, which I read in full from the item metadata. It runs: 'Historia calamitatum : Abelard to a friend : the story of his misfortunes -- The personal letters. Letter 1. Heloise to Abelard ; Letter 2. Abelard to Heloise ; Letter 3. Heloise to Abelard ; Letter 4. Abelard to Heloise -- The letters of direction. Letter 5. Heloise to Abelard ; Letter 6. Abelard to Heloise [summary] ; Letter 7. Abelard to Heloise ; Abelard's confession of faith -- Letters of Peter the Venerable and Heloise...'. So in this edition the Historia Calamitatum is printed under its own title and is NOT numbered as a letter; the numbered sequence begins with Heloise's first letter as Letter 1, and Abelard's reply is Letter 2. The verifier's stated reason for the number, 'The Penguin edition prints the Historia Calamitatum as Letter 1 and Heloise's reply as Letter 2', is contradicted by the edition's own contents.

WHERE THE NUMBER 2 COMES FROM, WHICH IS WHY THIS TRAP IS EASY TO FALL INTO. In the Latin numbering, Muckle's and Monfrin's, the Historia IS Epistola I and Heloise's first letter is Epistola II, and a great deal of scholarship cites it as Letter 2 on that basis. Both numbers are in honest use. But rule 4 requires the locator to work in the named edition, and rule 5 makes the named edition the one whose wording is used. The source line names trans. Betty Radice, 1974, so the number must be Radice's, and Radice's is 1. The fix is one character, and the source line stays at 101 characters or 109 with the publisher, inside the 140.

THE WORDING, WHICH IS SOUND AND WHICH I CHECKED PROPERLY. The verifier's only witness was a 2013 personal blog, which is not a text. I ran the line through OpenLibrary's full-text search of Internet Archive's scans instead. 'God knows I never sought anything in you except yourself' returns ten books, among them Penguin's own Great Loves volume Forbidden Fruit: From The Letters of Abelard and Heloise, which is a Penguin reprint of the Radice translation, with the snippet 'God knows I never sought anything in you except yourself; I wanted simply you,...'. 'I wanted simply you, nothing of yours' returns eighteen, including the same Penguin volume and Peggy Kamuf's Fictions of Feminine Desire, several of them continuing 'I wanted simply you, nothing of yours. I looked for no marriage-bond, no marriage portion...'. The semicolon the proposal carries is right and the full stop that the quotation sites print is wrong, so the verifier was correct on that point. Wording confirmed in a Penguin setting of Radice.

THE LETTER ITSELF, FOR THE CORRECTED CITATION. The sentence belongs to Heloise's first letter, the one that answers the Historia, not to her second. The continuation the snippets show, 'I looked for no marriage-bond, no marriage portion', is the refusal-of-marriage argument that Heloise makes only in the first letter, alongside the passage about preferring the name of mistress to that of wife and of empress; her second letter is about hypocrisy and the impossibility of repentance and contains no such argument. So Letter 1 in Radice, Epistola II in the Latin, and the corrected source line should say Letter 1.

WHAT I COULD NOT GET. The 1974 and the 2003 Penguin scans are both access-restricted, djvu.txt 401, so I never saw a printed page of either and cannot say whether Michael Clanchy's 2003 revision renumbers. That does not matter for this citation, which names 1974, but if the editor ever moves the source line to the 2003 revision the number must be checked again on the page.

SECONDARY GROUNDS, WHICH I WOULD NOT HAVE REFUTED ON ALONE, BUT WHICH THE EDITOR SHOULD WEIGH. First, theme. August is Impermanence, the passing of things. This is a declaration of constancy, the opposite movement: I wanted you and not what was yours. It is a superb line and it is not an August line, and it will read at six in the morning as a love letter, which it is. Second, the note is silent on the authorship question. The letters' attribution to Heloise has been contested since Charrier and Benton, and although the scholarly consensus now accepts her authorship, the house standard is to say plainly what is and is not settled; one clause would do it. Third, the note claims p. 51 'could not be confirmed', which is fine, but the source line and the note should not both be carrying an apology for a page nobody looked for; the letter number alone is a proper locator once it is the right letter.

EVERY OTHER GATE PASSES. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], heloise 0 of 3, not banned. Attribution to Heloise is standard and she is on no trap in the misattribution list. No speaker to name: a letter-writer in her own voice. Scope: twelfth century, Radice 1974, both before 1999, not scripture despite the monastic setting, not film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. Publishable. Tag Correspondence is the form of the work. Source line leads with the name, carries no dash, and ends in a full stop. Everything is right except the number, and the number is the thing a citation exists to get right.
